case_study_insert.main_stem: Westmore Kiln & Ceramics (WKM) is a cooperative in the industrial ceramics sector, employing a workforce of 70. Founded in 1987 by Elaine Westmore, it makes refractory bricks and kiln furniture for foundries and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. WKM plans to invest $640,000 in an energy-efficient kiln with waste-heat recovery, financed by a $340,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $260,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.50 a unit and a selling price of $22.50, and currently produces 50,000 units a year. WKM faces two problems: energy waste at the kiln is persistently high and its defect rate has reached 5.3%, worrying foundry customers.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Sustainability Report — Q1 2025: The kiln fired 9,600 refractory units last quarter with a defect rate of 5.3%, down from 7.0% last year, and broken units cost $23 each to remake. Energy waste accounts for 14% of kiln costs. Customer complaints rose from 17 to 29 per month. Average delivery time is 15 days. A survey of 220 construction and foundry buyers found that 66% would pay 2% more for low-energy ceramic products, and 54% check sustainability credentials. A skills audit shows 15 of 70 workers lack kiln-control certification; on-the-job training is available internally and off-the-job courses cost $860 per employee.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing loan costs for borrower-funded firms. (2) The national minimum wage rises 6.4% from $13.90 to $14.79 per hour from April 2026. (3) Natural gas and clay input costs have risen 10.8% year-on-year, inflation is 6.6%, and foundry output grew 2.4%.

questions.question_text: WKM plans to fund part of its $640,000 kiln project with a $340,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for WKM of using retained profit rather than the bank loan for this part of the investment.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The $300,000 of retained profit carries no interest or repayment, protecting cash flow while WKM already has fixed costs of $260,000 a year and energy waste equal to 14% of kiln costs. Money not paid to the bank can be spent on reducing the 5.3% defect rate and the $23-per-unit remake cost, or on the $860 kiln-control courses, helping the cooperative hold its $22.50 selling price and answer the 29 monthly complaints.

Point 2: Retained profit needs no collateral, so the $640,000 kiln is not at risk of repossession if foundry output, which grew only 2.4%, disappoints and the 50,000-unit plan is missed. It also suits WKM's cooperative structure: member-control is preserved because no lender can impose conditions on how the democratic leadership runs the business or reinvests surplus. Using internal funds therefore speeds the decision and keeps control with the members while the $340,000 loan remains available for other needs.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified, max 2.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to WKM's energy waste, defects, finance and ownership.

questions.question_text: WKM is promoting its new low-energy refractory products. Consider a foundry trade exhibition, direct mail to industrial buyers, or search-engine advertising. Which should WKM choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Foundry trade exhibition: A specialist exhibition would let WKM show the new kiln's output to foundry buyers face to face, supporting the 66% of 220 surveyed buyers who would pay 2% more for low-energy ceramics and allowing technicians to explain the 15-day delivery time. Yet exhibitions are costly in stands and staff time, and with fixed costs of $260,000 and a $340,000 loan, a poor event would be an expensive risk for a 70-member cooperative.

Direct mail: Sending technical brochures to a targeted list of construction and foundry buyers is relatively cheap and reaches the right firms, and can highlight the 54% of buyers who check sustainability credentials. Response rates are usually low and hard to track, however, and printed material can be ignored; it also does not demonstrate the product or the reduced energy waste, which is the central selling point of the $640,000 kiln.

Search-engine advertising: Paid search puts WKM in front of buyers actively looking for refractory bricks and kiln furniture, is measurable, can be budgeted to a 70-staff cooperative and can carry the 2% low-energy premium message and the 15-day lead time. It lacks the physical reassurance of an exhibition and depends on accurate keywords, but it delivers enquiries at a controllable cost and can be adjusted quickly if foundry output grows only 2.4%.

Recommendation: WKM should choose search-engine advertising as the main launch channel, with a small exhibition presence later. Search reaches active buyers cheaply and measurably, which matters against $260,000 fixed costs and a $340,000 loan. A full exhibition is rejected as too costly and risky, and direct mail alone is rejected as slow and low-response; successful online enquiries can fund a modest stand once the 5.3% defect rate is reduced.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the three promotional options with minimal application to WKM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of at least two options with advantages and disadvantages in the context of WKM and some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options applied to WKM with a justified recommendation explaining why exhibitions and direct mail alone are rejected.

questions.question_text: WKM's defect rate has reached 5.3% and complaints are rising. Explain two benefits for WKM of using democratic leadership to improve motivation among its kiln team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites WKM's 70 members to contribute ideas on kiln settings and defect prevention, which helps meet esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Operators who help design solutions are more likely to apply them carefully, reducing the 5.3% defect rate and the $23-per-unit remake cost and cutting energy waste that equals 14% of kiln costs. This fits a cooperative whose members expect a voice in decisions.

Point 2: Consulting the kiln team draws on practical experience that managers may lack, generating ideas to answer the 29 monthly complaints and to protect the 15-day delivery time, which matters because 66% of 220 surveyed buyers would pay a premium for low-energy products. Higher involvement also supports the $640,000 investment: with 15 of 70 workers lacking kiln-control certification, staff who feel heard are more willing to attend the $860 courses, and democratic decision-making reinforces Elaine Westmore's member-owned culture rather than imposing change from above.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified, max 2.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to WKM's defects, complaints, energy waste and structure.

questions.question_text: WKM must train 15 workers to control the new energy-efficient kiln. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job courses at the technical centre. Which should WKM choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the kiln is specific to WKM's own equipment and process, costs no course fees and keeps all 15 workers producing the 9,600 refractory units fired each quarter, protecting the 15-day delivery time and the effort to cut the 5.3% defect rate. Supervisors can show exactly how to reduce the 14% energy waste. The drawbacks are that trainers' own work suffers, that informal shortcuts may be passed on, and that no recognised certificate is provided even though 15 of 70 workers lack kiln-control certification.

Off-the-job courses: The technical centre course at $860 per employee gives structured kiln-control theory and a recognised qualification for all 15 workers, costing $12,900 in total, small beside the $640,000 kiln. It directly addresses the audit finding and supports the 54% of 220 buyers who check credentials and the 66% who would pay 2% more for low-energy products. However, it removes 15 of 70 staff from production, risking the 50,000-unit target and the 15-day lead time, and generic content may need site-specific follow-up.

Decision: WKM should choose off-the-job courses, reinforced by on-the-job coaching once staff return. Formal certification is the clearest answer to the 5.3% defect rate and the buyer requirement for credible low-energy production, and $12,900 is affordable within the $640,000 project. On-the-job training alone is rejected because it offers no certificate for the 54% of buyers who check credentials and may spread bad habits; the capacity loss can be managed by training in rotation. Losing 15 of 70 staff at once would be especially disruptive for a cooperative running a continuous kiln with a 15-day delivery promise.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to WKM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of WKM.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods applied to WKM with a justified decision covering certification, cost and disruption.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how WKM's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 26,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $10.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 24,000 units vs 50,000 output; modelling the 2% low-energy premium against $260,000 fixed costs; loan-service volume for the $640,000 kiln; and unit-cost benchmarking at $17.70 to cut the 5.3% defect rate and energy waste.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $260,000 ÷ ($22.50 − $12.50) = $260,000 ÷ $10.00 = 26,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 26,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $22.50 − $12.50 = $10.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $10.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways WKM's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 26,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 50,000 units, a margin of safety of 24,000 units, to judge whether the $640,000 kiln can be serviced from the $340,000 loan and $300,000 retained profit.
2. Contribution per unit of $10.00 lets WKM model the 2% premium that 66% of surveyed buyers would pay: 2% of $22.50 is about $0.45, lifting contribution to $10.45 and showing how quickly the kiln could pay back.
3. Fixed costs of $260,000 and contribution of $10.00 set the volume needed to cover loan interest and show how much of the 2.4% growth in foundry output the cooperative must capture.
4. Average total cost ($260,000 ÷ 50,000 units + $12.50 = $17.70 a unit) gives a benchmark for the 5.3% defect rate, the $23 remake cost and the 14% energy waste, and a base for negotiating the 10.8% rise in gas and clay prices.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii), max 4.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate WKM's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has WKM's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.65 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.64 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.89 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.99 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $175,000 inventories + $145,000 trade receivables + $60,000 cash = $380,000; 2025 current assets = $160,000 + $170,000 + $72,000 = $402,000. Short-term cover for 2024 is $380,000 ÷ $230,000 = 1.65 and for 2025 is $402,000 ÷ $245,000 = 1.64. Excluding inventories, ($380,000 − $175,000) ÷ $230,000 = 0.89 in 2024 and ($402,000 − $160,000) ÷ $245,000 = 0.99 in 2025.

Evaluation: The picture is mixed but the underlying trend is better. Overall short-term cover slipped slightly from 1.65 to 1.64 because current liabilities rose from $230,000 to $245,000 while current assets increased only from $380,000 to $402,000. However, the acid test improved from 0.89 to 0.99 because inventories fell from $175,000 to $160,000, so WKM is much less dependent on selling stock to pay debts, which matters while it services a $340,000 loan and installs a $640,000 kiln. The offsetting concern is trade receivables rising from $145,000 to $170,000, tying up cash; if foundry customers pay late after the 15-day delivery, cover could weaken. The $640,000 kiln has lifted non-current assets from $2,100,000 to $2,480,000, so the cooperative is committing more cash to fixed capacity while receivables rise; that is why the acid-test improvement matters more than the small dip in overall cover.

Conclusion: WKM's financial position has improved overall. The slight dip in overall cover is more than offset by the acid-test improvement and lower inventories, so liquidity is less stock-dependent; the real weakness is higher receivables, so the cooperative should tighten credit control before committing more cash.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether WKM's position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for WKM of installing waste-heat recovery on its new kiln.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Waste-heat recovery would cut the energy that is currently 14% of kiln costs, directly reducing the pressure from the 10.8% rise in gas and clay input costs and lowering the $17.70 average total cost. It supports the 66% of 220 surveyed buyers who would pay 2% more for low-energy ceramics and the 54% who check sustainability credentials, helping WKM sell the 50,000 units at $22.50 and defend the $640,000 investment.

Disadvantage: The recovery system adds capital cost and technical complexity to a project already funded by a $340,000 loan and fixed costs of $260,000 a year, raising risk if foundry output grows only 2.4%. With 15 of 70 workers lacking kiln-control certification and a defect rate of 5.3%, poor operation could cause temperature faults that raise the $23 remake cost and the 29 monthly complaints, while maintenance downtime could threaten the 15-day delivery time. WKM's members would also need training on the new controls, and 15 of 70 workers are not yet kiln-certified.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to WKM's energy, survey and investment data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.25%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.8% rise in natural gas and clay input costs will affect WKM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): If WKM's $340,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $340,000 = $2,550 a year (0.0075 × $340,000), modest next to fixed costs of $260,000, and zero if the loan is fixed. Dearer credit may also discourage foundry investment beyond the forecast 2.4% output growth, but WKM can largely remove this risk by fixing the loan rate at outset.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $14.79 per hour): With a workforce of 70, many kiln and packing roles are hourly paid, so the wage bill rises unavoidably. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual figure can honestly be calculated; the defensible check is productivity of 50,000 units ÷ 70 staff = 714 units per worker. If that holds, the $10.00 contribution can absorb the rise; if defects of 5.3% reduce effective output, unit labour cost will push up the $17.70 average total cost.

Input cost inflation (10.8% gas and clay): The $12.50 variable cost includes these inputs, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 10.8% that adds 10.8% × $12.50 = $1.35 per unit, about $67,500 a year at 50,000 units (50,000 × $1.35). Waste-heat recovery and the 2% price premium accepted by 66% of buyers can offset part of this, but not all of a broad rise.

Conclusion: The 10.8% rise in gas and clay input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 50,000 units and directly erodes the $10.00 contribution that must cover $260,000 fixed costs and service the $340,000 loan. The interest rise is small and fixable, and the wage rise can be managed through productivity; input inflation is the change WKM can least control and therefore bites deepest.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to WKM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on WKM's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes applied to WKM with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
